title: The volatile keyword
context: What does volatile guarantee, and what does it not?

source.title: JavaGuide (Snailclimb): Java concurrency questions (2 of 3)
source.note: Question and topic from this JavaGuide article. The answer is an original English write-up; see content/sources/javaguide/NOTICE.md.

answer: A volatile field guarantees visibility: a write is seen by all later reads of that field, and reads and writes are not reordered around it in a way that breaks the happens-before rules. It also makes a long or double read and write atomic. It does not make compound actions atomic: `count++` is three steps, read, add and write, so two threads can lose an update. For that use AtomicInteger, a lock, or synchronized. Use volatile for a simple flag or a published immutable reference.

points.title: Visibility, not atomicity
points.why: volatile makes writes visible, but count++ on a volatile field still loses updates.

points.title: Ordering
points.why: A volatile write happens-before a later read of the same field.

points.title: Good use
points.why: A stop flag or a safely published reference suits volatile.
